baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Schooling, school inspection and the census studied as state formation in the Canadas: education as 'government of the self' (1988), inspection as the making of 'relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (1992), the census as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001); work that predates the framework, and that Christie later cites for the point that McKay describes governmentality (2009)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: In-period reviews, read in full; Curtis's books are unread, so his words are the reviewers' quotations with their page references. Davey (Historical Studies in Education 1, 1989, pp. 161–165) on Building the Educational State (1988): 'one of the great strengths of Curtis' approach is his grounding of Foucault's analysis of power and subjectivity within a marxist theory of state formation and cultural forms' (p. 161); he quotes Curtis that 'the construction of the Educational State was accomplished only through the destruction of a prior educational organization and the marginalization of the structure of educational possibilities' (book p. 15), that schooling meant 'the anchoring of the conditions of political governance in the selves of the governed' (no page given), that education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (book p. 110) and that 'public education was administered into dominance only through a myriad of local struggles' (book p. 132); Davey notes 'there is no reference to Gramsci or the theory of hegemony in the bibliography or the index' (p. 162) and objects that Curtis 'fails to provide an adequate account of patriarchal relations in the period' (p. 165). Miller (Historical Studies in Education 5, 1993, pp. 123–126) on True Government by Choice Men? (1992) quotes 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (book p. 32) and 'Bureaucratic administration was seen by political liberals as practical education, a ‘normal school’ for the people' (book p. 7); she says Curtis 'carefully distances himself' from a social-control argument (p. 124) and regrets 'the relative invisibility of gender relations' (p. 125). Bryan Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, pp. 365–367): 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); yet he credits Curtis and Colonial Leviathan with 'the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366). Later readings: Belshaw (2002, read) quotes the census book: 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305). Christie (Underhill Review 2009, read): 'Here I think we need to be alert to Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality'; this is Christie's characterisation, and Curtis's own 2009 chapter ('After ‘Canada’') is unread. The edge records a contribution to the strand the atlas calls 'State formation before the framework'; the work predates McKay's prospectus (2000, unread beyond its abstract), and no checked text by McKay names Curtis. The collaboration with Philip Corrigan (1985) is title-level; the moral regulation entry treats this state-formation work as shared ground (edge_848), so no separate Curtis edge to moral_regulation is drawn.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Census returns read as artefacts of state knowledge rather than transparent records: objections to inferring property, gender and inheritance from the 1871 Ontario census in a review of Darroch and Soltow (1996), and census making as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Curtis's 1996 review of Gordon Darroch and Lee Soltow's census study of property in Ontario (1994) and his census history (2001); it is not a verdict on quantitative history as a whole, and Darroch and Soltow are not in the atlas. His own words (Historical Studies in Education 8, 1996, pp. 107–110, read in full): 'Anyone who has worked with manuscript census data must be impressed with the meticulous and painstaking analysis undertaken here' (p. 109); 'Two related critical points seem worth making about census artifacts and the matter of gender' (p. 109); the authors 'go so far as to suggest that their cross-sectional study is actually longitudinal' (p. 109); 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns, although, as an ideological practice, census-taking attached property to adult men' (pp. 109–110); and, qualifying, 'the book is an important contribution to ongoing debates' (p. 110). The census book (2001) is unread; as Belshaw quotes it (2002, read), 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305), and it 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26). Belshaw's reading, in his words: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout', and 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'. Kind: critique, because the 1996 text objects to inferences drawn from census returns; it is not a rejection of quantitative work, and Curtis calls the book he reviews an important contribution.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Canada as a project of liberal rule: the prospectus of 2000
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (2000). The prospectus abstract (read) proposes mapping 'the Canadian state as a project of liberal rule in northern North America' to get beyond the 'socio-cultural versus national-political impasse'. Its core formulation (pp. 620–21) is checked as quoted by Fecteau (2009): 'Canada-as-project can be analyzed through the study of the implantation and expansion over a heterogeneous terrain of a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism.' The prospectus body is not read here. McKay's spring 2000 Acadiensis essay (pp. 90–91, read) sets out the same programme in his own words: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; the project 'was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. A contribution, not a founding: state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it, and Pâquet (2009) names Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources. In the sampled corpus, 90 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the prospectus. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. The 2009 reply and the histories of the left (2005, 2008) are later readings, not evidence for this edge.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Colonial Leviathan (1992, edited with Ian Radforth): mid-nineteenth-century state formation in the Canadas, written before the framework was named, and later faulted by Greer himself for neglecting Indigenous peoples (2019)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Colonial Leviathan is unread (lending-only copy; the Érudit, Left History and Histoire sociale reviews returned bot checks). In-period reading: Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, read in full) says the volume and Curtis's book 'are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada' (p. 365) and finds that 'the collection lacks coherence', while its 'single most important contribution ... also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); he names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (p. 366). Valverde's 1992 essay cites Fecteau's chapter in the volume (edge_966). Greer's own later judgment (2019, read): 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84). Comparison only: the volume predates McKay's prospectus (2000), and no checked text by McKay or his commentators names it; Pâquet (2009) links the framework to studies of state formation in general. The atlas's state_formation_roots strand places it there editorially.
